value.overview: The Yellow-billed Cuckoo (Coccyzus americanus) is a slender, long-tailed cuckoo of the Americas. It breeds mainly in the eastern and central United States and migrates south for the nonbreeding season. Its populations are especially associated with deciduous woodland, woodland edges, dense second growth, and streamside vegetation. The species is known for its distinctive knocking or rolling calls and for feeding heavily on large caterpillars during outbreaks of insects.
value.classification: The Yellow-billed Cuckoo belongs to the order Cuculiformes and family Cuculidae. It is one of several North and Central American cuckoos in the genus Coccyzus.
value.identification: This medium-sized cuckoo has warm brown upperparts, clean white underparts, a long graduated tail, and a slightly decurved yellow bill with a darker tip. The underside of the tail shows broad white spots or bands separated by black. In flight, the wings can show a noticeable rufous or reddish flash. Adults have a yellow eye-ring and dark facial markings. It is often difficult to see because it sits quietly among foliage and moves unobtrusively through trees and shrubs.
value.rangeHabitat: The Yellow-billed Cuckoo breeds mainly across the eastern and central United States, with smaller western populations, and winters largely in South America. During migration and the nonbreeding season it uses forest edges, riverine woodland, second-growth vegetation, shrubland, hedgerows, overgrown farmland, orchards, and other habitats with dense foliage and nearby water. In Costa Rica it is a rare and local migrant or nonbreeding visitor, recorded particularly in suitable lowland and foothill habitats rather than being a common resident or breeding species.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds breeding in North America move south in late summer and autumn, pass through Central America, including Costa Rica, and winter mainly east of the Andes in South America. Costa Rica supports the species only rarely and locally during migration and the nonbreeding season.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs primarily in North America, not normally in Costa Rica. Pairs build a small, loose platform nest of twigs in shrubs or low trees, usually in dense vegetation. Both adults participate in nest construction, and the female lays a small clutch of pale bluish or greenish eggs. Incubation and nestling periods are short, and young birds leave the nest at an early stage. In some populations, breeding may increase when abundant caterpillars provide plentiful food.
value.dietFeeding: Large caterpillars are an important food, including tent caterpillars, fall webworms, and other moth larvae. The cuckoo also eats beetles, cicadas, katydids, crickets, ants, grasshoppers, spiders, small frogs, lizards, eggs, and occasionally small fruits. It usually forages by moving slowly through foliage and taking prey from leaves and branches, but may also drop to the ground to capture animals. Fruit becomes more important outside the breeding season.
value.behavior: The Yellow-billed Cuckoo is generally secretive and spends much of its time motionless in leafy cover. It often feeds alone and may remain difficult to detect even when calling. Its characteristic calls include deep, knocking or rolling notes and softer cooing sounds. It can be active during daylight and, during migration, may travel through woodland patches and over open areas using rapid, fluid wingbeats. Its movements and breeding activity can be strongly influenced by outbreaks of large insects.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered decreasing. Declines are uneven across the range, with eastern populations generally more numerous and western populations more restricted and vulnerable.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include loss, degradation, and fragmentation of riparian woodland, deciduous forest, and dense second-growth habitat. Water diversion, river regulation, agricultural conversion, development, removal of streamside vegetation, pesticides, and climate-related changes can reduce food supplies or suitable habitat. Migratory and wintering populations may also be affected by habitat loss in Central and South America, including the rare and local population occurring in Costa Rica.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore riparian forests, woodland edges, mangroves, and dense native second-growth vegetation. Maintain connected habitat along rivers and wetlands, reduce unnecessary pesticide use, and support conservation of migratory stopover and wintering areas. In Costa Rica, recording sightings through reputable bird-monitoring programs can improve knowledge of this uncommon migrant and help identify important local habitats.
